L968@P27: 2.6 UWB channels and preamble codes
L969@P27: The IEEE802.15.4 standard [1] has 16 defined channel/bands for the HRP UWB PHY. The DW3000 supports
L970@P27: the subset of these listed in Table 8 below. Depending on the channel and the pulse repetition frequency
L971@P27: (PRF) the IEEE802.15.4 standard [1] HRP UWB PHY defines a choice of two or four preamble codes. The
L972@P27: standard defined preamble code options are also listed in Table 8. The combination of channel number and
L973@P27: preamble code is what the standard terms a complex channel.

L988@P27: The preamble codes specified by the standard for use on a particular channel were chosen to have a low
L989@P27: cross correlation factor with each other with the intention that the complex channels could to operate
L990@P27: independently from each other as separate networks. In practice, as there is still some cross correlation,
L991@P27: there will be some break-through between different codes especially in conditions of close proximity with
L992@P27: long preambles.
L993@P27: The IEEE802.15.4 standard [1] includes a feature called dynamic preamble select (DPS), where devices switch
L994@P27: to using one of the DPS specific preamble codes for the ranging exchange, and perhaps a different one for
L995@P27: each direction of communication. The idea is to make it more difficult to eavesdrop or spoof, by randomly
L996@P27: changing the DPS preamble codes in a mutually agreed sequence only known to the valid participants. This
L997@P27: is supported by the DW3000 where at 64 MHz PRF the preamble codes additionally available for DPS are: 13,
L998@P27: 14, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23 and 24.
L999@P27: 2.7 Data modulation scheme
L1000@P27: The UWB specified in the IEEE802.15.4 standard [1] is sometimes called impulse radio UWB because it is
L1001@P27: based on high speed pulses of RF energy. During the PHR and Data parts of the packet, information bits are
L1002@P27: signalled by the position of the burst, in a modulation scheme termed burst position modulation (BPM).
L1003@P27: Each data bit passes through a convolution encoder to generate a “parity” bit used to set the phase of the
L1004@P27: burst as either positive or negative, this component of the modulation is termed binary phase-shift keying
L1005@P27: (BPSK). Figure 10 shows how the convolutional encoder contributes to this BPM/BPSK modulation. A
L1006@P27: coherent receiver (i.e. one tracking carrier timing and phase) such as the one in the DW3000 can determine
L1007@P27: this burst phase and use it in a Viterbi decoder to get an additional 3 dB of coding gain, thereby extending
L1008@P27-28: the operational range of the modulation.DW3000 User Manual
L1009@P28: © Decawave Ltd 2019 Version 1.1 Page 29 of 255
L1010@P28: Figure 10: BPM/BPSK data and PHR modulation
L1011@P28: In addition the quarter symbol interval is sub-divided into 2, 4, or 8 sub-intervals and a pseudo random
L1012@P28: sequence used to determine both the burst shape and which of the sub-intervals are actually used for the
L1013@P28: burst transmission. This gives more immunity to interference and whitens the output spectrum allowing a
L1014@P28: higher signal power to be used in the transmitter.
L1015@P28: Forward error correction (FEC) is also included in the PHR and Data parts of the packet. The 19-bit PHR
L1016@P28: includes a 6-bit single-error-correct double-error-detect (SECDED) code and the data part of the packet has a
L1017@P28: Reed Solomon (RS) code applied. Both SECDED and RS codes are termed “systematic” meaning that the data
L1018@P28: can be recovered without using the codes (and of course not benefitting from them in that case), e.g. by a
L1019@P28: non-coherent receiver. The 850 kb/s and 6.8 Mb/s user data rates quoted, include allowance for the 0.87
L1020@P28: average RS coding rate. The PHR is not RS coded so for example at the 850 kb/s nominal rate the PHR is
L1021@P28: actually sent at 975 kb/s.

L2226@P61: 6 Secure ranging / timestamping
L2227@P61: One of the main features of the DW3000 (differentiating it from the DW1000) is its secure timestamping
L2228@P61: ability.
L2229@P61: The timestamping ability of the DW1000 is based on accumulated correlation of the repeated symbols of the
L2230@P61: 802.15.4 standard preamble sequence. Please refer to the IEEE 802.15.4 standard [1], for more details of
L2231@P61: the packet format. When the SFD is detected a coarse receive timestamp is taken and then the accumulator
L2232@P61: state, which essentially provides the radio channel impulse response, CIR, is used to find the first arriving ray
L2233@P61: of RF energy and adjust the RX timestamp to give the sub-nanosecond precision achieved by the IC.
L2234@P61: Since the CIR accumulation is based on a repeated symbol of a known sequence of pulses defined by
L2235@P61: preamble code, it is possible for an attacker to send this same symbol (set of pulses) with a time offset which
L2236@P61: makes it appear like an earlier arriving ray in the CIR, and thus confuse the IC into reporting an earlier arrival
L2237@P61: time for the message. This could, for instance, foreshorten a ranging result, thus fooling an access system
L2238@P61: into thinking the user is closer than he actually is.
L2239@P61: To remove the possibility of such an attack the DW3000 has the ability to include a scrambled sequence in
L2240@P61: the packet, which can be used to obtain an RX timestamp that cannot be attacked in this way. This
L2241@P61: scrambled timestamp sequence (STS) is generated in accordance with the IEEE 802.15.4z amendment [2],
L2242@P61: and consists of a sequence of randomised pulses generated by an AES-128 CPRNG (cryptographic pseudorandom number generator) block in counter mode. This is also termed a deterministic random bit generator
L2243@P61: (DRBG). Only valid transmitters and receivers know the correct seed (i.e., key and data) to generate the
L2244@P61: sequence for transmission and for reception to cross correlate and accumulate to produce a CIR estimate
L2245@P61: from which to determine the RX timestamp.
L2246@P61: When the STS modes are enabled the DW3000 transmitter will insert the STS in the position shown in Figure
L2247@P61: 13, and the receiver will expect it to be present accordingly. The STS is generated by the AES-128 block
L2248@P61: output and is determined by a seed consisting of a 128-bit key, and a 128-bit nonce (a number that should
L2249@P61: only be used once). The nonce is updated during the STS generation by incrementing the counter once for
L2250@P61: every 128 pulses produced. When transmitting and receiving devices are using aligned seeds (i.e., same key
L2251@P61: and nonce) with the counter values aligned, the receiver generates a secure version of the CIR by correlating
L2252@P61: with the matching scrambled pulse sequence. The resultant timestamp is thus secure against attack.
L2253@P61: Figure 24: STS structure
L2254@P61: As shown in Figure 24, the STS consists of an active segment bracketed at either end by a gap (of 512 chips
L2255@P61: or approx. 1 μs). The length of the STS (active segment) is specified in units of 512 chips (~1 μs). In BPRF
L2256@P61: mode, where the STS pulse spacing is 8 chips, the mandatory STS length of 64 units has an active segment of
L2257@P61: 4096 pulses. For convenience we sometimes call this 512-chip (~1 μs) period an STS symbol.

L10925@P247: This appendix is for information only and describes various methods of implementing a two-way ranging
L10926@P247: scheme between two nodes.
L10927@P247: The chosen two-way ranging algorithm is implemented by host system software and is not a feature of the
L10928@P247: DW3000. The DW3000 just provides the facilities for message time-stamping and precise control of message

L10967@P248: 12.3 Double-sided two-way ranging
L10968@P248: Using four messages
L10969@P248: Double-sided two-way ranging (DS-TWR) is an extension of the basic single-sided two-way ranging in which
L10970@P248: two round trip time measurements are used and combined to give a time-of-flight result which has a
L10971@P248: reduced error even for quite long response delays.
L10972@P248: Figure 32: Double-sided two-way ranging with four messages
L10973@P248: The operation of DS-TWR is as shown in Figure 32, where device A initiates the first round trip measurement
L10974@P248: to which device B responds, after which device B initiates the second round trip measurement to which
L10975@P248: device A responds completing the full DS-TWR exchange. Each device precisely timestamps the transmission
L10976@P248: and reception times of the messages.
L10977@P248: Using three messages
L10978@P248: The four messages of DS-TWR, shown in Figure 32, can be reduced to three messages by using the reply of
L10979@P248: the first round-trip measurement as the initiator of the second round-trip measurement. This is shown in
L10980@P248: Figure 33.

L1053@P29: coherent receiver to determine the exact impulse response of the RF channel between transmitter and
L1054@P29: receiver. This brings two important benefits. Firstly, it allows the receiver make use of the received energy
L1055@P29: from multiple paths, turning multipath from an interference source into a positive affect extending operating
L1056@P29: range. Secondly, it lets the receiver resolve the channel in detail and determine the arrival time of the first

L1140@P32: 3.1 Basic transmission
L1141@P32: The transmission of packets is one of the basic functions of the DW3000 transceiver. The packets can be sent
L1142@P32: both with and without data payload. The DW3000 supports four packet formats, the IEEE802.15.4 standard
L1143@P32: [1] packet format, and three new IEEE802.15.4z amendment [2] defined formats where a scrambled
L1144@P32: timestamp sequence (STS) is introduced into the packet as shown in Figure 13. When the STS modes are
L1145@P32: enabled the DW3000 transmitter will insert the STS in the position shown, and the receiver will expect it to
L1146@P32: be present accordingly. The packet begins with a synchronisation header consisting of the preamble and the
L1147@P32: SFD (start of frame delimiter). The PHY header (PHR) defines the length (and data rate) of the data payload
L1148@P32: part of the packet. The STS when inserted allows for secure timestamping, and ranging, see § 6.
L1149@P32: Figure 13: Packet formats
L1150@P32: The DW3000 basic transmit sequence is as shown in Figure 14, beginning in the IDLE_PLL state awaiting
L1151@P32: instruction from the host controller.
L1152@P32: In order to transmit, the host controller must write data for transmission to TX_BUFFER, and select the
L1153@P32: preamble length, frame length, data rate and PRF in the Transmit Frame Control and Channel Control
L1154@P32: registers, TX_FCTRL and CHAN_CTRL. The PRF will be set according to the chosen preamble code
L1155@P32: (TX_PCODE). Assuming all other relevant configurations have already been made, the host controller
L1156@P32: initiates the transmission by issuing a TX command (e.g. CMD_TX). Once transmission is initiated, the
L1157@P32: DW3000 sends the complete packet of preamble, SFD, PHR and the PHY Payload (MAC Frame). The STS will
L1158@P32: be included optionally depending on the configured packet format (see Figure 13). In the STS packet
L1159@P32: configuration 3 (SP3) the PHR and PHY Payload is omitted.
L1160@P32: As an aid to MAC layer framing, the IC calculates the FCS (CRC) during the transmission of the (MAC) data
L1161@P32: from the TX_BUFFER based on the frame length (TXFLEN) and automatically appends it.

L1206@P34: For delayed transmission, the transmit time is programmed into DX_TIME and then the delayed transmission

L2348@P64: received packet through the RX_STAMP field in Sub-register 0x00:64 – Receive time stamp. To ensure the
L2349@P64: integrity of the receive timestamp based on the STS, the user must check that the CP_TOAST quality status
L2350@P64: indicator (in CP_TS) is not indicating any issues with the STS CIR analysis.
L2351@P64: NB: The host should not attempt to read ACC_MEM until the CIA has finished its processing, (as signalled by
L2352@P64: the CIADONE event status flag), since this may give rise to a conflict with the CIA accesses to the CIR memory
L2353@P64: which may interfere with the generation of a good RX timestamp result.
L2354@P64: Note: It is also very important to assess that quality of the STS accumulation before accepting that a receive
L2355@P64: timestamp CP_TOA value is sufficiently good enough to be trusted in a two-way ranging exchange. This is a
L2356@P64: unitless value that summarizes the results of the STS quality algorithm that is monitoring the reception of
L2357@P64: the STS. For high signal levels this measurement should be very high but its value will reduce as the signal
L2358@P64: level reduces. An ACC_QUAL value (in STS_STS) that is <60% of the STS length indicates that the reception of
L2359@P64: the STS was too poor for the first path analysis to obtain a reliable ToA and so the received timestamp based
L2360@P64: on STS should not be trusted.

L2362@P64: 128 (i.e. CPS_LEN is set to 15), the STS based receive timestamp (CP_TOA) value should only be trusted when
L2363@P64: the STS accumulation quality (CPS_ACCQUAL) value is greater than ≥ 77 (i.e. 60 % of 128).
L2364@P64: As mentioned above STS uses a continually varying sequence. This means that a colliding packet will not line
L2365@P64: up with the desired signal. As a result, the ToA will be unaffected. If security is not a concern, then overhead
L2366@P64: of key management and counter control is undesirable. For this reason, the DW3000 includes a special STS
L2367@P64: mode that uses a code optimized for ToA performance. This is known as the Super Deterministic Code
L2368@P64: (SDC). If SDC is enabled (by CP_SDC bit), then the STS will be populated with the SDC code. Since it is a time
L2369@P64: varying sequence optimized for ToA performance it will better tolerate packet collisions without requiring
L2370@P64: any key management.
L2371@P64: It is important to remember that the SDC mode does not provide security but will increase confidence in the
L2372@P64: ToA when the on-air packet density is high. For this reason, we would recommend that an SDC based STS is

L1426@P39: Data demodulation
L1427@P39: Section 2.7 – Data modulation scheme describes the modulation scheme. In the receiver a Viterbi decoder is
L1428@P39: used to recover the data bits (this is also used for PHR reception) which are then passed through the Reed
L1429@P39: Solomon decoder to apply, if it can, any further corrections. Every octet thus received is passed through a
L1430@P39: CRC checker that checks the frame against the transmitted FCS.
L1431@P39: As the data octets are received they may also be parsed by the frame filtering function if enabled, see
L1432@P39: section 5.4– Frame filtering for more details.
L1433@P39: Successful reception of a frame is signalled to the host via the RXFR and RXFCG event status bits in
L1434@P39: SYS_STATUS. Other status bits in this register may be used to flag reception of other parts of the frame or,
L1435@P39: events indicating failure, i.e. RXPTO (Preamble detection Timeout), RXSTO (SFD timeout), RXPHE (PHY
L1436@P39: Header Error), RXFSL (Reed Solomon error), RXFTO (Frame wait timeout), etc.

L1442@P40: RX message timestamp
L1443@P40: The IEEE802.15.4 standard [1] nominates the time when the RMARKER arrives at the antenna as the
L1444@P40: significant event that is time-stamped, also shown in Figure 13.
L1445@P40: The DW3000 digital receiver circuitry takes a coarse timestamp of the symbol in which the RMARKER event
L1446@P40: occurs and adds in various correction factors to give a resultant adjusted time stamp value, which is the time
L1447@P40: at which the RMARKER arrived at the antenna. This includes subtracting the receive antenna delay as
L1448@P40: configured in the RXANTD register (in CIA_CONF) and adding the correction factor determined by the first
L1449@P40: path (leading edge) detection algorithm embedded in the DW3000. The resulting fully adjusted RX
L1450@P40: timestamp is written into RX_STAMP, IP_TOA and STS_TOA registers.
L1451@P40: See also section 10.3 – IC calibration – antenna delay, and section 6 – Secure ranging / timestamping.
